params.notes: This is the problem the benchmark addresses. Most benchmark scores ask whether the model produced the right answer and report a single number. In a clinic, the deliverable is judged three other ways. First, in physical units: a registration of the pre-operative MRI to the ultrasound is only useful if landmarks line up within about 2 millimetres; an organ mask matters because of the volume in millilitres; a risk score has to be calibrated, meaning a predicted 20 % risk should come true about 20 % of the time. Second, in time: a pipeline that needs an hour per scan cannot be used during surgery. Third, against a specialist: the fair bar is the dedicated system a hospital would use, run on the same hidden cases, not a leaderboard from another dataset. Transition: so we built tasks that measure all three.
params.title: Clinical evaluation — what a generic benchmark score leaves out

params.notes: Here is how every task works, left to right. The agent, Claude Code with web tools removed, gets a workspace with a clinical README, development cases with their reference answers, and network access only to the model API. It has 30 to 60 minutes and one attempt. What it must leave behind is not an answer but a pipeline: a run.sh that takes an input folder and writes the clinical output, offline. A separate verifier, which the agent never sees, runs that pipeline on hidden cases under a clinical time limit, scores the output in clinical units against a published threshold, and compares it with a specialist system's stored outputs on the very same cases. The five tasks below span imaging and signals: registering brain MRI to intra-operative ultrasound, a CT spleen mask with its volume, fetal head circumference from ultrasound, a five-class 12-lead ECG model with calibration and subgroup checks, and ICU mortality risk. Each card shows the clinical bar, the time limit and how the specialist did; note the specialists are not perfect either, passing 4 of 6 and 3 of 6 cases on the two small imaging tasks. Transition: here is how the two frontier models did.

Turquoise is Claude Opus 5.5, pink is Claude Sonnet 5.5, and the yellow diamond is the specialist on the same cases. The counts on the right are Opus, Sonnet, specialist. Three things to say. One: on fetal head circumference, a measurement in millimetres, both models fall clearly short of the specialist. The specialist is within tolerance on all 83 hidden images, Opus on 35 and Sonnet on 64. The paired differences and their 95 % intervals are well below zero, so this is a gap under our rule. Two: Opus matches the specialist on registration and on the spleen; on registration its mean error is actually lower, 1.61 versus 3.03 millimetres. But with only 6 hidden cases, and 4 or 3 that the specialist passes, 'no gap' here means 'not enough data to show one', not proof of parity. Three: ECG and ICU risk are controls: everybody passes every part of the gate, which shows the harness is not simply too hard. One more fact for questions: every hidden case finished within its time limit, so all lost reward is clinical, not delivery failure. Transition: let us look at the fetal head gap image by image.

params.notes: The exact gap rule and every verdict. For the per-case tasks we take only the hidden cases the specialist passes, called S, and compute agent minus specialist pass rate with a paired bootstrap interval. A gap is claimed only when the agent fails at least one of those cases and the whole interval is below zero. Fetal head shows a gap for both models with intervals far from zero. Registration for Sonnet is a gap because it failed all four; the interval is degenerate at minus one. Opus registration and Sonnet spleen fail some specialist-passed cases but, with 4 and 3 cases, the interval reaches zero, so we say 'no gap shown' and call it underpowered rather than reassuring.
params.title: Gap verdicts — paired differences on specialist-passed cases

params.notes: Where each clinical bar comes from. Registration and spleen bars come from published clinical accuracy and inter-observer studies; the fetal head tolerance is the inter-observer limit between sonographers; the ECG myocardial infarction operating point comes from the classic CSE study; the ICU bar is the challenge's own score against the SAPS-I baseline. Where no published number existed, for example the 90 % family bar or the calibration bounds, we declared our own convention before any agent ran and say so.
